summary: This informational memo helps vendors and participants at trade shows such as Networld+Interop design effective protection against network and system attacks by unauthorized people.

plainLanguage.summary: Tips for locking up your stall at a busy fair so nobody tampers with your things.

subtitle: Practical security checklist for vendors exhibiting at network trade shows.

tldr.problem: Systems at trade shows face the same attack risks as office systems, but security is often overlooked because exhibits are temporary and focused on demonstrations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides a checklist of straightforward, frequently overlooked security measures—physical controls, password practices, service hardening, and network filtering—designed specifically for the trade show environment.
tldr.outcome: Vendors who follow these practices significantly reduce the chance of breaches that could disrupt their demonstrations and damage their brand.

facts.label: Main risks
facts.value: Unattended systems, weak passwords, unnecessary services, unfiltered network access

facts.label: Key controls
facts.value: Physical security, hardened passwords, packet filtering, authentication tokens or encryption

today: RFC 2179 is an Informational RFC from July 1997. It remains a relevant checklist of good security practices for temporary deployments and shared network environments. Many recommendations (such as using strong passwords, keeping software updated, and monitoring access) are still standard practice today.

sections.title: Why Trade Show Security Matters
sections.content:
A trade show like Networld+Interop brings together vendors to showcase products and services. It also concentrates potential attackers in one place: competitors, curious researchers, and opportunists. The RFC notes that systems at trade shows are as vulnerable to attack as office systems, yet security is frequently overlooked because booth staff focus on demonstrations and view the setup as temporary.

A security breach can render demonstrations inoperable for the entire event, embarrassing the vendor and potentially lasting damage to customer relations. The RFC's goal is not to be comprehensive, but to provide a checklist of simple, commonly overlooked measures that significantly raise the bar against attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: At a big fair full of tech companies, thousands of tech-savvy people are nearby. If you don't lock things up, someone will notice and may try to mess with your demo.

sections.title: Physical and Personnel Security
sections.content:
Physical security is the foundation. The most dangerous vulnerability is a console left logged in as root. An attacker with physical access and an active root session has complete control of a system, and can modify system files or steal data.

The RFC recommends educating booth staff about this risk: never leave a system with an active login unattended, and do not allow anyone to log in as root on a booth machine except in an emergency. Be skeptical of anyone requesting access for "maintenance"—verify their identity before granting access to systems. Do not allow staff to give out passwords, even if the requester claims to be from the company or from the show organizers.

Identify individuals using booth systems for purposes other than intended demonstrations. Restrict system access to authorized personnel during the trade show.
sections.plainLanguage: Don't leave your laptop with "admin" logged in, and ask for ID before letting strangers use your machines.

sections.title: Hardening Systems Before the Show
sections.content:
Before shipping systems to the trade show, perform basic hardening steps:

Passwords: Many systems ship with default or null passwords, especially for privileged accounts. Change all passwords, especially root. Use passwords that mix uppercase, lowercase, numbers and symbols, and avoid passwords related to the event, company, or products. Set passwords on all user accounts—systems should not have any accounts with null passwords.

Privileged accounts: Some systems ship with multiple accounts that have root privileges. Disable extra privileged accounts by placing an asterisk (*) in the password field of /etc/passwd (on Unix). Restrict root login to the system console only, not over the network, using /etc/securettys or equivalent controls.

Unnecessary services: Disable or remove services not needed for the demonstration. Remove the notorious "R services" (rsh, rexec, rlogin), TFTP, anonymous FTP, and NFS exports unless specifically required. Check for suid (setUID) binaries in unusual locations and remove them if they are not needed.

File permissions and ownership: Verify that system directories like / and /etc are owned by root, not by user accounts. Check for world-writable directories like /tmp and ensure their permissions are appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you go: change all passwords, delete extra admin accounts, turn off services you don't need, and fix file permissions.

sections.title: Network Services and Monitoring
sections.content:
At a trade show, there are many packet sniffers running on network segments, both legitimate (exhibitors analyzing their products) and not. Assume that any unencrypted password sent across the network will be captured.

Authentication: Use authentication tokens (like SecureID or Cryptocard) that generate one-time passwords. These are useless after a single use, rendering captured sniffed passwords worthless. Alternatively, use SSH (Secure Shell) which encrypts the connection, making both passwords and data unreadable to sniffers.

Network services: Use packet filtering to restrict incoming connections. A good approach is to deny everything by default and allow only specific services explicitly needed. Block spoofed packets by validating source addresses at the border. Block source-routed packets unless specifically needed. Allow established TCP connections but block new inbound connection requests except to specific needed services.

Specific service blocks: Block the "R-command" ports (512-515) used by rsh/rexec/rlogin. Block telnet (port 23) except to hosts that specifically need it. Block TFTP (port 69). Allow only necessary services like DNS (port 53), FTP for specific servers (port 20), SMTP for mail servers (port 25).

Monitoring: Use TCP Wrappers (tcpd) to restrict and monitor TCP connections by host, logging unauthorized access attempts. Examine log files regularly using the last command for recent logins and syslog or Event Viewer for system events. Monitor web server logs for access patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Don't send passwords in plain text. Use encryption or one-time passwords. Block network ports you don't need. Watch the logs.

sections.title: Web Server and Software Security
sections.content:
Web servers are frequent targets. Remove or disable any CGI scripts not needed for demonstrations, especially utilities like phf that have been exploited to read system files. All scripts in the cgi-bin directory should be reviewed for security. Consult the operating system vendor for the latest version of all software, especially sendmail (which has had many security holes) and BIND (DNS daemon). Apply all available security patches before deploying systems.

Share network files only when necessary. Do not provide writable NFS exports; if NFS is needed, export read-only and verify what information is visible. Similarly, be careful with other file-sharing protocols like CIFS, AppleShare or NetWare.

Check trusted hosts files (/etc/hosts.equiv and .rhosts) for open entries ('+' allows all hosts). Remove "xhost +" from X11 configuration. These files are common vectors for unauthorized access.

Good backups are essential. Make a backup before the show, continue backups during the event, and backup again after. A final backup set is useful to investigate potential break-ins after the show.
sections.plainLanguage: Update software, remove test scripts, back up your data, and don't leave file shares wide open.
